subject: Dedicated commit exceedance: metering, throttles, and settlement

Subject: Question on committed GPU pool behaviour when we exceed our commit

Hannah,

Thanks again for the demo last week — Acme is excited about moving some of our inference traffic onto a dedicated pool. Before we finalize the SOW, two quick clarifying questions from procurement/ops:

1) If our production traffic spikes and we exceed the committed GPU pool (for example, sustained 30% above commit for 3 hours), how is that charged and enforced? Do you immediately throttle requests, queue, or automatically bill overage?

2) What is your metering window for detecting spikes — instantaneous, 5-min, hourly? We need to map this to our incident playbooks.

3) Any example invoice math or sample scenarios you can share so procurement can sign off?

We have a short procurement window next week; appreciate a succinct answer and any supporting examples.

Best,

Elena — thanks for the clear questions. I pulled in engineering, sales, and billing so we can give you operational and commercial options rather than a single yes/no. High-level summary up front, followed by specifics and an example file attached (dedicated-pricing-examples.xlsx).

Summary (options):
- Soft-burst allowance: automatic short bursts up to a configured % (we commonly offer 15–25% for the first 60–90 minutes) that incur metered usage at the committed unit rate (or a small uplift) to avoid spurious throttles.
- Metered overage with smoothing: usage is measured by GPU-minute (primary) with a 5-minute sliding window to detect immediate spikes and a 24-hour smoothing window for billing/true-up.
- Throttle tiers: after burst allowance is exhausted, we apply progressive throttling by pool (not by request) with transparent notification and optional failover to a lower-cost model variant.
- Monthly true-up: default commercial path is a monthly invoice true-up; we also offer a capped overage option for customers who prefer pre-approved burst credits.

Key details:
- Metering unit: GPU-minute (we compute equivalent GPU-minute for multi-accelerator instances). We also correlate token counts per request for cost attribution and quality alerts.
- Detection windows: 5-minute sliding window triggers immediate burst detection; 1-hour and 24-hour windows used for automated smoothing and to avoid charging for short anomalies.
- Billing math: we provide two commercial flavors — immediate overage billing at a per-GPU-minute uplift, or monthly true-up with tiered pricing. See the spreadsheet for 3 scenarios (short spike, sustained surge, and month-end ramp).
- SLA/behavior during exceedance: we can guarantee throughput up to commit. For exceedances: 1) short bursts — best-effort with burst allowance; 2) sustained excess — optional throttling or model-fallback policy (if configured) to preserve core traffic.

Attachments: dedicated-pricing-examples.xlsx (spreadsheet) — example invoices and two proposed commercial templates.

Next steps I propose: 1) we review the preferred commercial template (Option A: monthly true-up; Option B: capped burst credits + overage uplift), 2) we include a short MSA clause for measurement windows (we've started a draft and will circulate), and 3) engineering and Acme ops validate the 5-min window for alerts.

If useful, we can produce a sample May invoice using your recent telemetry — just share a CSV.

Quick technical notes from runtime team to make the options concrete. TL;DR: metering and throttles are implementable, but behavior under sustained overcommit requires trade-offs that you (Acme) should accept explicitly (degraded latency or fallback models).

1) Metering and windows: we record GPU allocation per request and aggregate into GPU-minutes. For burst detection we use a 5-minute sliding window (this keeps sensitivity to short bursts). For billing smoothing we compute a rolling 24-hour average and a monthly true-up. That allows us to avoid billing for a 2‑minute anomaly while still capturing sustained spikes.

2) Throttling semantics: throttles are applied at the pool-level, not at the per-API-key level, to preserve fairness across tenants sharing the same pool. A soft-throttle reduces token concurrency and increases queue time; a hard-throttle returns a 429. We recommend a progressive approach: soft-throttle -> model-fallback -> hard-throttle.

3) Failover: if Acme configures model-fallback, we can automatically route to a quantized / lower-memory variant with lower throughput but lower GPU cost. That preserves request success rates at the expense of latency or slight quality degradation.

4) Meter reconciliation: for auditability, we emit per-minute usage logs and a daily summary. We can provide an S3/Drive export for your finance team.

I attached an initial MSA language snippet to this thread (Hannah, I uploaded the draft to the shared drive). Happy to iterate on exact thresholds.

-Aditya

Subject: Commercial options for exceedance handling — two proposals

Elena — following the engineering and ops notes, here are two commercial templates that map to the operational behavior Hannah outlined. I included a simple CSV that walks through a May billing example (acme-billing-scenario.csv).

Option A — Monthly true-up (recommended for customers who prefer predictable invoices):
- Metering: GPU-minute, 5-min sliding trigger, 24-hour smoothing for billing.
- Billing: Monthly true-up at 1.5x committed unit price for overage up to 100% of commit during the month; 2.5x beyond that.
- Cap: optional negotiated cap (e.g., 150% of commit) available for an additional fixed monthly fee.

Option B — Pre-approved burst credits (recommended for spike-heavy use cases):
- We provide N GPU-hours of burst credits per month (negotiable; example: 30 GPU-hours).
- Short bursts within credits charged at committed unit price; once credits are exhausted, overage billed at 1.75x.
- If usage stays above commit for >24 hours, we switch to monthly true-up and engage throttling and model-fallback as per engineering notes.

Discounting and term: for a 2-year commit we can apply a 30% off list baseline; for a 3-year commit we can increase to 35% and include a one-time pool sizing review.

Legal/billing ask: Laura, can you draft the clause for the MSA that references the 5-min/24-hr windows and includes sample invoice math?

Attachments: acme-billing-scenario.csv (example math)

Cheers,
